definition: In this historical social-psychology usage, Gemeinschaft refers to a kind of human grouping that overlaps with what the source calls “company”: a group held together more by sympathy, instinct, impulse, or other unreflective bonds than by deliberate, formally organized social relations. Tönnies contrasts it with Gesellschaft, or society.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Company; pinned source text

reasons: The packet describes Baldwin’s technical meaning for “company” as groupings formed by “sympathy, instinct, or impulse, rather than by thought,” but it does not state that “Gemeinschaft” *overlaps with* that same “company” sense; it only says Tönnies makes a “partially coincident distinction” between Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft.

The definition adds “deliberate, formally organized social relations” and “other unreflective bonds,” which are not explicitly supported by the packet’s wording (the packet mentions “without formal organization” and “rather than by thought,” but not the specific contrast phrasing used in the definition).
